# **Hardening Ultra-Low-Power Cascaded Acoustic Wake-Up Systems Against the Sim-to-Real Gap**

Deploying always-on voice interfaces within strict energy and memory budgets presents an asymmetric systems challenge: the device must maintain sub-milliwatt standby power while rejecting ambient acoustic interference1. In a two-stage cascaded architecture on an ARM Cortex-M0+ microcontroller, such as the Raspberry Pi RP2040, Stage 1 typically executes a continuous hardware-level matched filter or voice activity detector directly on a 1.024 MHz 1-bit Pulse Density Modulation stream, while Stage 2 invokes an INT8-quantized Depthwise Separable Convolutional Neural Network operating on 16 kHz decimated audio within a 16 KB SRAM budget4.  
The primary barrier to field deployment is the "sim-to-real gap," where classifiers trained on clean speech and synthetic stationary noise suffer catastrophic degradation when exposed to physical environments4. Bridging this gap requires replacing synthetic artifacts with calibrated physical channel modeling, testing against standardized acoustic corpora, hardening the front-end against mechanical transients, and aligning the training pipeline with integer microcontroller arithmetic4.

## **1\. Real-World Acoustic Noise Benchmarks and Corpora**

Early speech enhancement literature relied heavily on legacy corpora such as NOISEX-92, which evaluated systems using stationary white Gaussian noise, pink noise, and continuous vehicle rumbles4. In modern embedded sensor systems research targeting venues such as ACM SenSys, IEEE/ACM IPSN, and IEEE ICASSP, evaluations relying exclusively on NOISEX-92 or synthetic Gaussian perturbations are routinely rejected4. Synthetic stationary noise lacks the multi-path spatial reflections, non-stationary temporal envelopes, localized bursts, and spectral dynamics found in natural acoustic scenes4. Evaluating an edge wake-up pipeline against synthetic baselines leads to severe over-optimism: systems that report greater than 95% clean keyword accuracy frequently collapse under live conditions where additive noise exhibits time-varying non-stationarity and harmonic overlap with human speech4.  
Modern peer-reviewed literature mandates benchmarking against high-fidelity environmental corpora that capture acoustic dynamics across multi-channel or high-resolution spatial recordings4. The Diverse Environments Multi-channel Acoustic Noise Database (DEMAND) provides calibrated multi-channel recordings across sixteen real-world settings categorized into domestic, office, public, transportation, nature, and street acoustic scenes13. For single-channel 1-bit PDM systems, DEMAND provides standardized background noise profiles that include diffuse reverberant noise and authentic spatial reflections13.  
The WSJ0 Hipster Ambient Mixtures (WHAM\!) dataset supplies non-stationary background noise captured in restaurants, bars, and coffee shops using binaural microphones, providing realistic overlapping conversational babble and localized domestic transient clatter17. Complementing these are the MUSAN corpus, which provides over one hundred hours of categorized non-verbal vocalizations, diverse musical genres, and ambient sound effects, and ESC-50, which isolates discrete impulsive acoustic events20.  
Reviewers expect wake-up pipelines to be evaluated systematically across distinct environmental categories, each isolating specific failure mechanisms in the cascaded architecture4. Cafeteria and restaurant babble constitutes a mandatory test category because overlapping speech shares the fundamental frequency (![][image1]) range, formant envelopes, and syllabic cadence of target wake words, challenging the phonetic discrimination of the Stage 2 classifier4. Industrial machine halls and workshops present heavy, continuous low-frequency harmonics below 500 Hz, unmodulated motor whine, and periodic metallic impacts, testing whether low-frequency energy saturates the input accumulator or causes clipping in the 1-bit PDM hardware stage23.  
Transit and traffic environments, including subways and vehicles, exhibit wide dynamic ranges, acoustic Doppler shifts, and infrasonic road rumblings that test whether high-amplitude out-of-band energy degrades baseband Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR)4. Finally, office and domestic spaces combine continuous HVAC fan rumbles with discrete, high-kurtosis mechanical transients such as typing and door strikes, testing the false-alarm resistance of low-power front-ends16.

## **2\. Sim-to-Real Acoustic Modeling**

Clean speech corpora such as Google Speech Commands consist of dry, near-field vocalizations recorded across varied microphones in isolated conditions5. Propagating these synthetic or dry commands to an embedded microphone requires modeling the physical acoustic channel, including multi-path reflection, geometric attenuation, boundary absorption, and calibrated sound pressure levels5.  
The physical transformation of a dry vocalization ![][image8] into a microphone-incident pressure waveform ![][image9] is governed by convolution with a room impulse response ![][image10], accompanied by additive background noise ![][image11], expressed as ![][image12]. The impulse response ![][image10] comprises direct acoustic propagation, early specular reflections occurring within 50 ms of sound arrival, and late diffuse reverberation decaying exponentially over time14. The duration of this decay is defined by the reverberation time ![][image13], the interval required for acoustic energy density to drop by 60 dB following signal cessation14. Realistic indoor deployments require modeling reverberation times within the range ![][image14], spanning damped living spaces to highly reverberant conference rooms14.  
The volumetric properties of simulated physical enclosures are governed by Sabine's classical formula:  
![][image15]  
where ![][image16] represents the speed of sound in air (![][image17] at ![][image18]), ![][image19] is the room volume in cubic meters, ![][image20] is the area of boundary surface ![][image21], and ![][image22] is its acoustic absorption coefficient, yielding the total absorption area ![][image23] in metric Sabins14. In spaces with elevated wall absorption, Eyring’s formula provides a more accurate formulation:  
![][image24]  
Simulations using packages like pyroomacoustics apply the Image Source Method (ISM) to place virtual mirror sources across boundary planes14. While ISM accurately calculates early reflection arrival times and amplitudes, relying exclusively on geometric mirror reflections creates artificial comb-filtering patterns in the frequency domain because physical surfaces scatter sound non-specularly14.  
A realistic sim-to-real pipeline must employ a hybrid simulation approach. Early reflections (![][image25]) are synthesized using low-order image source calculations with frequency-dependent surface absorption across standard octave bands from 125 Hz to 4 kHz14. Late diffuse reverberation (![][image26]) is synthesized using stochastic ray-tracing or exponentially decaying Gaussian noise matching the target ![][image13] decay envelope modulated by Rayleigh surface scattering14.  
To capture real-world non-idealities that geometric models omit—such as edge diffraction, furniture occlusion, and acoustic enclosure resonances—synthetic simulations must be augmented with measured physical RIR databases, such as the BUT Reverb Database or ACE Challenge corpora.  
A common methodological flaw in synthetic acoustic benchmarking is mixing speech and noise using naive Root-Mean-Square (RMS) amplitude calculations across entire audio files11. Because speech contains silence, unvoiced stop closures, and inter-syllable pauses, whole-file RMS calculations integrate extended periods of zero signal energy, drastically underestimating the true acoustic power of active vocalizations11. Consequently, adding noise scaled against whole-file speech RMS creates an active signal-to-noise ratio that is substantially higher than the nominal parameter, yielding overly optimistic evaluation results that degrade under live microphone conditions11.  
Accurate sim-to-real audio mixing requires calibrating audio power to physical Sound Pressure Levels (referenced to ![][image27]) and calculating speech power according to the ITU-T Recommendation P.56 Method B (Objective Measurement of Active Speech Level)11. Conversational speech at a distance of one meter corresponds to ![][image28], shouting reaches ![][image29], and quiet commands drop to ![][image30]. Additive background noise spans quiet offices (![][image31]) to crowded restaurants (![][image32]) and traffic corridors (![][image33]), establishing an operational target SNR envelope between ![][image34] and ![][image35]23.  
The standardized audio mixing pipeline operates across four sequential phases:

Second, the active speech power ![][image37] is determined via ITU-T P.56 Method B11. The reverberant signal is passed through an envelope detector with an exponential smoothing time constant of ![][image38]37. The algorithm tracks signal activity relative to an active speech threshold ![][image39] set exactly 15.9 dB below the active speech level margin, updating iteratively until the computed power matches the integrated energy within active intervals27.

Summing the signals yields the mixed digital waveform ![][image47], which matches physical pressure levels and avoids synthetic testing bias11.

## **3\. Non-Speech Acoustic Transient Robustness (Rejection of False Triggers)**

A major point of failure in low-power acoustic wake-up systems is the vulnerability of the Stage 1 detector to non-speech impulsive transients1. In the RP2040 system, the hardware front-end interfaces with a 1.024 MHz 1-bit PDM digital MEMS microphone using a Programmable I/O (PIO) state machine that clocks the microphone line and samples the 1-bit data stream into FIFO queues7.  
Stage 1 processes this bitstream using an unweighted boxcar decimation popcount across rolling windows or monitors pulse-density transitions to estimate baseband signal power8. While computationally efficient, this simple energy tracking cannot differentiate between phonemic speech formations and non-speech acoustic shocks1.  
Mechanical door slams and structural thuds generate low-frequency shockwaves below 100 Hz that displace the MEMS diaphragm, generating runs of consecutive identical bits that saturate the popcount accumulator despite having no speech content23. Handclaps and finger snaps produce sharp acoustic shocks with rise times under 1 ms and crest factors exceeding 15 dB, easily triggering static energy thresholds49.  
Cutlery impacts, plate drops, and key rattles generate resonant high-frequency acoustic bursts between 3 kHz and 8 kHz, producing rapid bit-flip sequences that mimic unvoiced fricatives such as /s/ and /sh/. Mechanical typing and mouse clicks create periodic acoustic bursts that prevent energy-tracking integrators from decaying. Finally, non-speech physiological sounds such as coughs and throat clearing share vocal tract formants with human speech, frequently bypassing simple amplitude checks.  
When non-speech transients repeatedly trigger Stage 1, the microcontroller wakes its core and executes Stage 2 inference, increasing the duty cycle from an idle target below 1% to over 20%1. This repeated false activation drains system energy, negating the advantages of the cascaded design1.  
Suppressing these transients within the computational limits of the Cortex-M0+ requires combining hardware-assisted filtering with firmware-level validation routines:

\[1.024 MHz PDM Stream\]  
           │  
           v  
\[PIO State Machine: Dual-Edge Sampling & Run-Length / Delta-Density Filter\]  
           │  
           v  
\[DMA Transfer of Packed Bit-Words\]  
           │  
           v  
\[Dual-Band Fixed-Point Integrator\] ──(Sub-Band Energy Ratio Test)──\> Out-of-Band? ──\> \[Drop\]  
           │ (Pass)  
           v  
\[Adaptive Hangover Finite State Machine\] ──(Temporal Persistence Check)──\> \< 60 ms? ──\> \[Drop\]  
           │ (Pass)  
           v  
\[Wake Stage 2: 16 kHz INT8 DS-CNN Classifier\]

Human speech concentrates acoustic energy in the voice band between 300 Hz and 3.4 kHz. In contrast, door slams peak below 200 Hz, while cutlery drops and clicks concentrate energy above 4 kHz. Although the Cortex-M0+ core lacks single-cycle SIMD DSP instructions, it can execute low-order 16-bit fixed-point Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) filter banks on decimated samples: a voice-band bandpass filter (![][image48]) and an out-of-band rejection filter (![][image49]).  
Before triggering Stage 2, the firmware computes the ratio of in-band speech energy ![][image50] to out-of-band energy ![][image51]:  
![][image52]  
If ![][image53] falls below an empirically calibrated threshold ![][image54], the frame is classified as an out-of-band transient and discarded49.  
Acoustic transients also exhibit sharp attack and decay times (![][image55]), whereas spoken words require sustained energy across syllables lasting 150 ms to 400 ms. The Stage 1 detector enforces a temporal persistence requirement using a lightweight finite-state machine. The signal must maintain an energy level above an activation threshold ![][image56] for at least three consecutive frames (40 ms to 60 ms) before waking the Stage 2 classifier. Transients decay before meeting this threshold, resetting the accumulator.  
Conversely, when valid speech is detected, inter-phoneme pauses (such as stop closures before unvoiced plosives) can cause temporary energy drops. The state machine applies hangover logic, holding the active detection flag for 100 ms to 150 ms after the energy drops below a lower threshold ![][image57], preventing signal fragmentation and avoiding repeated microcontroller wake-up cycles37.  
Additional transient suppression can be implemented at the hardware boundary using the RP2040 PIO state machines7. Delta-sigma PDM modulators shift quantization noise upward into high frequencies, yielding smooth variations in pulse density for voice-band inputs. Wideband impulses and electrostatic discharges produce runs of alternating polarities or blocks of identical bits.  
The PIO state machine can track run-lengths of identical bits and count zero-crossings directly on the 1.024 MHz stream before data reaches the DMA channels7. If the zero-crossing rate exceeds boundaries derived from human speech (![][image58]), the PIO drops the audio block, preventing an interrupt from waking the Cortex-M0+ core7.

## **4\. Multi-Condition Data Augmentation for TinyML Models**

Deploying a keyword spotter within a 16 KB SRAM budget on a Cortex-M0+ requires an ultra-compact model topology5. A representative architecture is an INT8-quantized Depthwise Separable Convolutional Neural Network (DS-CNN) that takes an input spectrogram of 10 to 20 frames by 10 to 20 Mel-frequency cepstral bins and employs 24 to 32 channels per separable layer5.  
With fewer than 25,000 parameters, these ultra-compact networks have limited capacity9. Over-augmenting during training causes underfitting because the network lacks the capacity to resolve conflicting acoustic features4. Conversely, under-augmenting leaves the model vulnerable to domain shifts4. Hardening these networks requires multi-condition data augmentation tailored to low-capacity integer classifiers4.

Raw Speech Utterance  
         │  
         v  
\[Room Impulse Response (RIR) Augmentation\] ──\> RT60: 0.1s to 0.6s  
         │  
         v  
\[Dynamic Time-Stretch & Pitch Modification\] ──\> Shift: ±2 Semitones, Stretch: ±10%  
         │  
         v  
\[Dynamic Noise Injection\] ───────────────────\> Real Noise (DEMAND/WHAM\!), SNR: \-5 dB to \+20 dB  
         │  
         v  
\[Fixed-Point MFCC Feature Extraction\] ──────\> Emulates 16-bit Integer MCU DSP Math  
         │  
         v  
\[Conservative SpecAugment\] ──────────────────\> Max 2 Mel Bins, Max 4 Time Steps  
         │  
         v  
\[Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)\] ─────────\> Symmetric INT8, Clamped to \[-128, 127\]

Reverberation modeling convolves dry training utterances on-the-fly with randomized RIRs representing reverberation times between ![][image59] and ![][image60]14. This introduces the temporal smearing and formant distortion typical of physical rooms into the training distribution, preventing the network from relying on sharp spectral transitions present only in dry recordings.  
Pitch shifting (![][image61] semitones) combined with time stretching (![][image62] to ![][image63]) introduces variance in speaker fundamental frequency (![][image1]) and cadence. This broadens demographic coverage without requiring wider convolutional layers10.  
Additive noise from DEMAND, MUSAN, and WHAM\! is introduced dynamically during mini-batch generation rather than via pre-mixed offline files9. In each training epoch, noise sources are randomly mixed with clean speech at target SNRs uniformly distributed between ![][image34] and ![][image35] using ITU-T P.56 active speech power calculations11.  
The training pipeline must also include an explicit "Unknown / Negative" class containing hard non-speech transients from ESC-50 alongside background babble9. This trains the DS-CNN to reject non-target sounds that pass through the Stage 1 front-end22.  
SpecAugment provides strong regularization by zeroing blocks of time steps and frequency bins. However, standard SpecAugment hyperparameter ranges designed for large automatic speech recognition models can degrade performance on small-footprint networks. For an input feature map of ![][image64] Mel bins:

* Frequency masking must be restricted to at most one or two bins (![][image65]). Masking broader bands can remove entire formant trajectories, preventing the compact network from learning reliable phonemic features.  
* Time masking must be limited to two to four frames (![][image66]). Broader masks can obliterate short consonants or plosive bursts, erasing critical acoustic cues.  
* Time warping should be omitted entirely, as it incurs computational overhead during training while offering negligible generalization benefits for sub-second keyword spotting.

A subtle contributor to the sim-to-real gap is the divergence between double-precision floating-point feature extractors used in training frameworks and the fixed-point integer math executed on microcontrollers10. Because the Cortex-M0+ lacks a hardware floating-point unit, feature extraction runs using 16-bit or 32-bit fixed-point arithmetic (Q15 or Q31)10. Rounding operations, integer division truncations, and approximations in logarithm look-up tables introduce systematic biases into the resulting Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients12.  
Applying post-training quantization directly to a model trained on floating-point features frequently degrades performance when exposed to noisy inputs6. To preserve accuracy, training pipelines must use a bit-exact software emulator of the embedded fixed-point feature extraction routine12.  
Furthermore, the model must be trained using Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) with simulated INT8 arithmetic on all weights and activations54. Using Learnable Step Size Quantization (LSQ), the step size parameter ![][image67] is optimized alongside network weights, allowing activation ranges to adapt to the variance introduced by additive noise and reverberation54. Activations should be constrained using bounded non-linearities such as ReLU6 to prevent dynamic-range expansion, ensuring consistent quantization scaling across quiet and noisy conditions6.

| Augmentation Strategy | Parameter Tuning Bounds | Induced Invariance Mechanism | Impact on 16 KB INT8 DS-CNN |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **RIR Convolution** \[cite: 14, 24\] | ![][image68]; Volume: ![][image69] | Multi-path propagation and room boundary absorption | Prevents overfitting to sharp anechoic spectral envelopes; avoids temporal smearing failures. |
| **Dynamic Noise Mixing** \[cite: 4, 9\] | Acoustic SNR ![][image70] via ITU-T P.5611 | Additive ambient noise and conversational babble | Broadens decision boundaries across operational SNRs; limits noise-floor-induced accuracy drops4. |
| **Pitch & Prosody Perturbation** | Pitch: ![][image61] semitones; Time stretch: ![][image71] | Inter-speaker vocal tract length and speech tempo | Improves demographic generalization across pitch profiles without increasing model parameter counts10. |
| **Scaled SpecAugment** | **![][image72]** bins; ![][image73] frames | Channel dropouts, partial frequency occlusions | Provides regularization; helps prevent over-reliance on individual formants. |
| **Emulated Fixed-Point Math** \[cite: 12\] | Q15/Q31 fixed-point math, integer rounding | Alignment with Cortex-M0+ arithmetic10 | Eliminates classification discrepancies caused by differences between float32 training and integer inference54. |

## **5\. Reviewer Expectations and Paper Presentation (SenSys / IPSN)**

Systems conferences such as ACM SenSys and IEEE/ACM IPSN prioritize real-world hardware feasibility, comprehensive system-level evaluation, and verifiable energy tradeoffs over incremental gains in classification accuracy1. Presenting isolated accuracy numbers on the Google Speech Commands test set is insufficient for publication4. Reviewers look for end-to-end evidence demonstrating that the two-stage wake-up pipeline operates reliably, rejects real-world noise, and stays within the energy and memory bounds of the target microcontroller1.  
Evaluations must present Detection Error Tradeoff (DET) curves rather than standard linear Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) plots1. DET curves plot the Miss Rate (![][image74]) against the False Alarm Rate (![][image75]) on a normal deviate or logarithmic scale57. Because practical wake-up systems operate in low false-alarm regimes (![][image76]), standard linear ROC curves compress the region of operational interest into the plot boundary. DET curves spread this region across the graph, exposing trade-offs between competing operating thresholds under varying noise conditions1.  
System false triggers must be reported using the False-Wake Rate (FWR), measured in events per hour (![][image77])57. To satisfy reviewers, the experimental testbed must process continuous, unscripted multi-hour audio streams (typically 24 to 48 hours) comprising continuous speech, podcast conversations, television broadcasts, and domestic background noise13.  
System performance is characterized by plotting FWR in events per hour on the horizontal axis against Miss Rate on the vertical axis across varying classification thresholds. For edge deployments, an acceptable design point achieves an FWR below ![][image78] at a Miss Rate under ![][image79], with high-reliability targets requiring an FWR below ![][image80]50.  
Evaluations must also include parametric SNR degradation curves illustrating keyword detection accuracy and Stage 1 sensitivity across an SNR sweep from ![][image34] to ![][image35] in discrete 5 dB increments23. These sweeps should be broken down by environmental category (babble, industrial, traffic, HVAC) to illustrate where each stage degrades4.  
For cascaded wake-up systems, reviewers expect a rigorous energy waterfall model linking Stage 1 false triggers directly to overall battery lifetime1. Average system power is governed by:  
![][image81]  
where ![][image82] represents the continuous active power of the 1-bit PDM popcount front-end and DMA (![][image83] on the RP2040), ![][image84] is the active power drawn by the Cortex-M0+ core executing the INT8 DS-CNN at full frequency (![][image85]), ![][image86] is the inference execution latency (![][image87]), ![][image88] is the sliding frame step, and ![][image89] is the empirical activation rate of Stage 11.  
The paper must provide a parametric sensitivity plot demonstrating how elevated acoustic noise floors or frequent non-speech transients increase ![][image89], illustrating the resulting impact on projected battery lifetime1.

| Evaluation Dimension | Core Reported Metrics | Visual Representation Format | Common Rejection Vector |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Detection Reliability** \[cite: 1, 57\] | Miss Rate (![][image74]), False Wake Rate (![][image77])57 | Log-Log Detection Error Tradeoff (DET) curves1 | Reporting accuracy exclusively on pre-segmented 1-second test clips4. |
| **Acoustic Noise Resilience** \[cite: 4, 9\] | Recall and F1 score across ![][image34] to ![][image35] SNR23 | Parametric accuracy degradation sweeps per noise class54 | Evaluating only against stationary white Gaussian noise4. |
| **Transient Robustness** \[cite: 1, 42\] | Stage 1 Trigger Rate on non-speech events (ESC-50) | Confusion matrix of false wake activations by transient type | Omitting mechanical transients; failing to report live-environment false triggers1. |
| **Hardware & Systems Bounds** \[cite: 53, 55, 56\] | Peak SRAM buffer, flash usage, inference latency, Joules/inference | Memory layout breakdown; power and energy waterfall profiles55 | Reporting model parameter size while omitting feature extraction buffers55. |

Experimental designs should incorporate established methodologies from key acoustic and embedded systems literature. The architectural profile and parameter budgeting for microcontrollers should follow Zhang et al. (2017) in "Hello Edge: Keyword Spotting on Microcontrollers," which established baseline memory footprints, depthwise separable layer configurations, and operation counts for ARM Cortex-M hardware5.  
Environmental noise evaluation should adopt the standardized acoustic scenes defined by Thiemann et al. (2013) in "The Diverse Environments Multi-channel Acoustic Noise Database (DEMAND)," avoiding outdated stationary datasets13.  
End-to-end hardware measurement procedures should align with the MLPerf Tiny Benchmark Suite formulated by Banbury et al. (2021) and updated by the MLCommons Tiny Working Group (2025), which mandates logging latency and energy consumption across distinct pipeline stages: pre-inference feature extraction, neural inference, and post-processing53.  
Techniques for handling acoustic domain mismatch and on-device adaptation should follow Cioflan et al. (2021, 2024\) in "Efficient On-Device Domain Learning for Keyword Spotting on Ultra-Low-Power Platforms," which documents how DS-CNN topologies degrade under unseen noise and outlines hardening strategies for edge MCUs4.  
The mathematical formulation of the two-stage cascaded architecture should follow the Energy-Aware Neyman-Pearson framework established by Jun and Jones (2007, 2010\) in "An Energy-Aware Framework for Cascaded Detection" and "VLSI Implementation of an Energy-Aware Wake-Up Detector," which links false alarms to overall system energy consumption1.  
Finally, all audio mixing must follow ITU-T Recommendation P.56 (2011), "Objective Measurement of Active Speech Level," to ensure that speech energy calculations and SNR settings reflect physical acoustic realities11.

## **Conclusion**

Closing the sim-to-real gap for cascaded keyword wake-up systems on microcontrollers such as the RP2040 requires treating physical acoustic modeling, embedded signal processing, and quantized neural architecture design as an integrated system. Accurate simulation requires moving beyond synthetic noise additions to convolve clean training utterances with hybrid Room Impulse Responses covering representative reverberation times (![][image14]) and calibrating signal mixtures using ITU-T P.56 Active Speech Level normalization11.  
Hardware-level popcount front-ends must be hardened against high-energy, non-speech transients through multi-band energy ratio verification, zero-crossing bounds, and adaptive hangover logic, preventing mechanical shocks from triggering expensive Stage 2 inference1. For the Stage 2 INT8 DS-CNN classifier operating within a 16 KB SRAM footprint, training pipelines must combine conservatively tuned SpecAugment, dynamic noise injection, and emulated fixed-point feature extraction within Quantization-Aware Training to ensure numerical consistency with the integer microcontroller core5.  
Evaluating these systems to the standards of ACM SenSys and IEEE/ACM IPSN requires complementing traditional accuracy metrics with system-level Detection Error Tradeoff curves, continuous False-Wake Rates per hour, and cascaded power profiles that confirm long-term reliability in physical deployments1.
